name: Chain Bridge
description: The Széchenyi Chain Bridge, opened in 1849, was the first permanent bridge across the Danube in Hungary. Designed by an English engineer and built under a Scottish one, it carries stone lions at its abutments, was blown up in 1945 and rebuilt, and ties Pest's Széchenyi Square to Buda's Adam Clark Square.

children.text: The Széchenyi Chain Bridge links Buda and Pest across the Danube, anchored at Széchenyi Square on the Pest side and Adam Clark Square on the Buda side. It is a chain suspension bridge of wrought iron and stone, with cast-iron decoration. It opened on 20 November 1849 and was the first permanent bridge across the Danube in Hungary. Its centre span of 202 metres was among the largest in the world at the time, and the whole structure measures about 375 metres in length and 14.8 metres in width.

The design was drawn up in 1839 by the English engineer William Tierney Clark, and construction ran from 1840 to 1849. A Scottish engineer, Adam Clark, who was no relation to the designer, supervised the work on site and spent about ten years on it. Much of the funding came from the Greek merchant Georgios Sinas, whose name is inscribed on the base of the south-western foundation on the Buda side.

The building years were turbulent. During the 1848 revolution Clark helped the army of Lajos Kossuth cross the unfinished bridge; one estimate puts the number at 70,000 men and 300 artillery pieces in a single day. In early 1849 he flooded the anchorage chambers and disabled pumps to protect the bridge from an Austrian plan to blow it up, and only one of four gunpowder canisters detonated. In June 1849 he persuaded the Hungarian commander, General Henryk Dembiński, not to destroy the whole bridge. The platform was dismantled instead so that construction could resume later.

The sculptor János Marschalkó carved the stone lions at the abutments, installed in 1852. The bridge received its present name in 1898, and its iron structure was strengthened in 1914. Retreating German forces blew it up on 18 January 1945 during the Siege of Budapest, leaving only the towers standing; it was rebuilt and reopened in 1949. A popular story says the lions have no tongues, but Wikipedia calls this untrue and says the tongues are simply not visible from below.

On the Buda side, Adam Clark Square was renamed in 1912 in the engineer's honour and contains Hungary's Zero Kilometre Stone. The Buda Castle Tunnel, commissioned by the Hungarian government in 1850 and opened to foot traffic in March 1856, runs beneath the castle hill and comes out opposite the bridge. The Castle Hill Funicular also starts from the same square, so the crossing is a natural start for a walk up to the castle district.
Good to know
Walk across for views of Buda Castle and the Pest riverbank; the Pest end is at Széchenyi Square and the Buda end at Adam Clark Square.
Adam Clark Square holds the Zero Kilometre Stone, the mouth of the Buda Castle Tunnel and the lower end of the Castle Hill Funicular.
Look at the stone lions at the abutments and judge the tongue story for yourself; the tongues are said to be there but not visible from below.

historyIntro: Budapest's Chain Bridge became a lasting symbol of the connection between Buda and Pest long before the two cities were formally united.

historySections.heading: The bridge that changed how the city crossed the Danube

children.text: The Széchenyi Chain Bridge was the first permanent bridge connecting Buda and Pest across the Danube. It helped replace seasonal crossings with a reliable link between the growing communities on either bank.
The suspension bridge and its stone gateways remain central to the city's urban identity. The bridge was destroyed during the Second World War and later rebuilt.

name: St. Stephen’s Basilica
description: Budapest's largest church, named for Hungary's first king, took more than fifty years to build. Its 96-metre dome has a panoramic viewing platform, and the building is also a venue for organ concerts, so it works as both a place of worship and a lookout.

children.text: St. Stephen's Basilica is dedicated to Stephen I, the first king of Hungary, whose mummified right hand is kept in a reliquary inside. Construction began in 1851 and continued for fifty-four years. The first architect, József Hild, designed it in the neoclassical style; after his death in 1867 Miklós Ybl altered the plan toward the neo-Renaissance, and the work was completed by József Kauser. A dome collapse during construction forced much of the work to be rebuilt from the ground up, which is part of why it took so long.

At 96 metres the basilica is as tall as the Hungarian Parliament Building, and the two are often described as the city's equally high landmarks. The ground plan is a Greek cross. Pope Pius XI gave the church the title of basilica minor in 1931, and it is a co-cathedral of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Esztergom–Budapest.
Visitors can also go up to the dome: it can be reached by lift or by 304 steps, and from the top there are panoramic views over the city.

The basilica is also one of the city's regular concert venues, with organ concerts and other music programmes. Ticket options for the dome and the concerts differ, so check the official source for the current programme.
Good to know
The dome is reached by lift or 364 steps; the view is wide in clear weather.
Concert and dome tickets are separate from entering the church: check the current options before you go.
The Danube and the Hungarian Parliament are a short walk away.

historyIntro: One of Budapest's grandest churches, St Stephen's Basilica brings together nineteenth-century architecture and the story of Hungary's first king.

children.text: Construction extended across several generations and changes in architectural leadership. The building was completed and dedicated in 1905, becoming an unmistakable landmark of central Pest.
Its dome and richly decorated interior helped establish it as one of the city's major ceremonial spaces. Repairs and restoration have followed damage during the twentieth century.

The basilica is dedicated to Stephen I, the first king of Hungary. It houses the Holy Right, a relic traditionally identified as the king's preserved right hand, which remains important to Hungarian Catholic devotion.

stories.title: The Holy Right: a centuries-old religious tradition

children.text: The basilica tells the remarkable story of the Holy Right: according to Catholic tradition, the relic survived successive relocations and periods of concealment before being returned to public veneration.
This is a religious tradition associated with a preserved relic; claims of miraculous qualities belong to the tradition, not to verified scientific findings.

name: Matthias Church
description: Matthias Church is Buda's coronation church: a Gothic building of the 13th century, a mosque under Ottoman rule, and a showpiece of 19th-century restoration with a richly painted interior, beside Fisherman's Bastion on Castle Hill.

children.text: The church that crowns Castle Hill has served more than one faith and several rulers. Béla IV, between 1255 and 1269, replaced an older, smaller church with a three-nave basilica. Tradition credits an earlier foundation by Saint Stephen in 1015, but the sources note there is no clear evidence for it. The church takes its popular name from Matthias Corvinus, whose coat of arms on the south-west bell tower dates its rebuilding to 1470 (the earlier tower had collapsed in 1384), and who married here in 1463 and 1476.

It was also the coronation church of Hungary's later monarchs. Franz Joseph I and Elisabeth were crowned here in 1867, when Franz Liszt's Coronation Mass was first performed, and Charles IV and Queen Zita followed on 30 December 1916.

After the Ottomans took Buda the church was converted into a mosque, which it remained from 1541 to 1686. After the siege of 1686 the Jesuits restored it in Baroque style. The building you see today is largely the result of the restoration led by the architect Frigyes Schulek between 1874 and 1896, which gave it its steep Gothic spire and gargoyles.

Inside, the walls and vaults are covered with painted decoration, including murals by Bertalan Székely and Károly Lotz, with stained glass designed by them. The Ecclesiastical Art Museum begins in the crypt, and the church is also a concert venue, so a visit can combine sightseeing with music.
Good to know
Check opening arrangements before you go: the church is a place of worship and can close for services and events.
Fisherman's Bastion and the equestrian statue of Saint Stephen are directly beside the church.
Look up: the painted vaults and the pulpit reward a slow visit.

historyIntro: Behind Matthias Church's patterned roof is a long history of coronations, royal celebrations, religious changes and painstaking restoration on Castle Hill.

children.text: The Church of Our Lady on Buda Castle Hill is documented as under construction in the mid-thirteenth century. King Matthias Corvinus was closely associated with the church and celebrated both of his marriages here.
During Ottoman control of Buda in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the church was used as a mosque. It was returned to Christian worship after the reconquest of Buda in 1686.

historySections.heading: A church rebuilt for a new age

children.text: In the nineteenth century, architect Frigyes Schulek oversaw a major restoration that reshaped the building's appearance. Franz Joseph and Elisabeth were crowned Hungarian king and queen in 1867, and Hungary's last king, Charles IV, was crowned here in 1916.
Damage during the Second World War led to further restoration. The church remains both an active place of worship and a major historical landmark.

In 1309 Charles I was crowned in the church; the church's own chronology calls the crown provisional, while other sources describe a newly consecrated crown. His coronation with the Holy Crown of Hungary followed at Székesfehérvár in 1310.
The episode reflects how the correct crown and ceremony were central to the legitimacy of medieval Hungarian rule.

name: Buda Castle District
description: Castle Hill is the historic heart of Buda: a UNESCO-listed ridge of palace, churches and museums above the Danube, rebuilt after sieges and war, with views across the river to Pest. The Royal Palace, Matthias Church and Fisherman's Bastion all lie within a short walk of one another.

children.text: The first royal residence on Castle Hill was built between 1247 and 1265 under King Béla IV. Over the following centuries the palace was extended again and again: under Sigismund in the 1410s and 1420s, and, after his marriage to Beatrice of Naples in 1476, by Matthias Corvinus, who rebuilt it in an early Renaissance style.

Buda fell to the Ottomans in 1541, and the siege that ended Ottoman rule in 1686 destroyed the medieval palace. A small Baroque palace followed in the 18th century and was enlarged under Maria Theresa, finished in 1769. After fires in the 1849 siege the palace was rebuilt and expanded in the late 19th century to designs associated with Miklós Ybl and Alajos Hauszmann, and the Royal Palace was officially inaugurated in 1912.

The siege of Budapest in 1944–45 left the palace in ruins. Its post-war reconstruction, externally complete by 1966 although the interiors were finished only in the 1980s, took a simplified Baroque form and gave the building the outline and the dome you see today. Some medieval rooms were also uncovered and reconstructed.

Today the palace houses the Hungarian National Gallery, the Budapest History Museum and the National Széchényi Library. The streets around it, with Matthias Church, Fisherman's Bastion, Trinity Square and the Hospital in the Rock, form the Buda Castle Quarter, which is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing 'Budapest, including the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue', inscribed in 1987.

The district is compact and best explored on foot. Many visitors spend a half-day on the terraces, Matthias Church and Fisherman's Bastion, and add a museum or the Hospital in the Rock to make a full day.
Good to know
The Castle Hill Funicular climbs from Clark Ádám tér beside the Chain Bridge; walking up from the river is the alternative.
The museums in the palace have their own tickets and opening days: check each one before you go.
Matthias Church, Fisherman's Bastion and the Hospital in the Rock are all within a few minutes' walk of the palace.

historyIntro: Castle Hill has served as a royal, administrative and residential centre for centuries. Its present skyline contains medieval foundations, baroque rebuilding and modern reconstruction.

children.text: The Castle District began as a walled town on Castle Hill, founded by King Béla IV after the Mongol invasion of 1241–42, and the royal court soon settled in the growing town. Successive rulers, sieges and political changes reshaped its buildings and the surrounding walls.
Today the palace courtyards, historic lanes, churches and viewpoints preserve different moments of Budapest's history in a compact area.
